Focused Question — The Teachings of Muhammad vs. Jesus (and the Two Systems)

By request: Muhammad and his doctrines, Christianity as a system, and a like-for-like comparison of what Muhammad and Jesus actually taught. The dossier's rules apply — sources weighed by date, claims tested symmetrically, value-premises left to the reader.

1. The sources problem (stated first, for both)

  • Jesus' teaching: the only primary witnesses are the first-century Gospels — early, but theologically shaped (esp. John's high-Christology sayings; see cap. 05).
  • Muhammad's teaching: three layers — the Qurʾan (earliest, ~7th c.), then Ḥadīth (compiled 2nd–3rd c. AH, with an entire Muslim science of authentication, and much disputed material), then the Sīra (Ibn Isḥāq via Ibn Hishām, al-Ṭabarī — written ~150+ years later). Mainstream historians (Sean Anthony, Fred Donner) treat the Qurʾanic layer as primary and the Sīra cautiously.

Neither founder's words reach us unmediated. Symmetry: a skeptic's standard for the Gospels must also apply to Ḥadīth/Sīra, and vice versa.

2. Muhammad's core doctrines

  • Tawḥīd: absolute oneness of God; shirk the gravest sin.
  • Prophethood & finality: a line of prophets (Adam→Jesus), Muhammad the seal (Q 33:40); the Qurʾan as God's literal, final speech.
  • *Worship & law (the dīn): the Five Pillars (creed, prayer, alms, fasting, pilgrimage) and a comprehensive Sharīʿa* covering worship, family, contracts, criminal and political life.
  • Community & polity: the umma; Muhammad was simultaneously prophet, statesman, judge, and military commander (Medina period).
  • Ethics: charity (zakāt/ṣadaqa), care for orphans and the poor, honesty, justice, sexual morality, accountability at the Judgment, mercy (raḥma) as God's foremost trait.
  • *Regulated warfare (qitāl/jihād): a contested topic — the Qurʾan has both "no compulsion in religion" (Q 2:256) and the "sword" verses (Q 9:5; 9:29) in the context of 7th-c. Arabian conflict; Muslim scholarship splits between contextual/defensive and universalist readings, and over abrogation*. Presented as a genuine internal debate, not a settled polemic.

3. Jesus' teaching (per the Gospels)

  • The Kingdom of God is the center: it has drawn near; repent and believe.
  • The Sermon on the Mount: internalization of Torah ("you have heard… but I say"), the Beatitudes, love of enemies, non-retaliation ("turn the other cheek"), radical forgiveness, secret almsgiving.
  • Two great commands: love God (the Shema, Mark 12:29–30) and love neighbor; the Golden Rule.
  • Grace and the lost: parables of the prodigal, the lost sheep; forgiveness of sinners; warnings to the self-righteous.
  • His own role: "Son of Man" sayings, authority to forgive sins, the cross self-interpreted as "a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) — the high-self-claims being contested within scholarship.
  • Religion and power: no law code, no army, no state — "my kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36); executed by Rome, not ruling it.

4. Like-for-like comparison

DimensionJesus (Gospels)Muhammad (Qurʾan/Sīra)
Primary roleitinerant teacher-healer; suffering Messiahprophet and statesman, judge, commander
Core messageKingdom of God, grace, atonementtawḥīd, final revelation, a God-ordered society
Ethic of forcenon-resistance, enemy-loveregulated, sometimes offensive, warfare
Lawreinterprets Torah; no new codea comprehensive Sharīʿa
Religion & stateseparated ("not of this world")integrated (dīn wa dawla in practice)

Shared ethicsmonotheism, charity, mercy, justice, care for the poor, sexual morality, judgment to comesame list — substantial overlap

The ethical overlap is large; the structural divergence is the type of founder: a non-resistant suffering teacher vs. a prophet- statesman who also legislated and led in war.

5. The symmetry traps (both polemics fail here)

  • "Muhammad waged war, Jesus did not." True of the two individuals. But the honest comparison of scriptural systems must set Muhammad beside the Hebrew Bible's prophets and lawgivers — Moses, Joshua, David — and the Torah's *divinely-commanded ḥērem (Deut 20:16–17; 1 Sam 15:3, "kill man and woman, infant and nursling"). By that like-for-like measure the Bible's sanctioned warfare is at least as severe. Christian polemic that cites the Qurʾan's war verses while ignoring Deut 20 / 1 Sam 15 fails the symmetry rule* (Methodology §3).
  • "The Bible is violent, so Christianity is false." The Muslim mirror- polemic fails identically: OT war texts read out of their context, and Jesus' non-resistance ignored.
  • "As practiced" cuts both ways and is not the text. Crusades/ Inquisition vs. conquests — communities, not scriptures. The dossier judges texts, and flags "as-practiced" arguments as off-target on both sides.

The defensible residue: Jesus' personal recorded ethic is distinctively non-resistant; Muhammad's recorded career is that of an armed prophet- statesman — but so is Moses'/David's. So the sharp contrast is Jesus-the-individual vs. Muhammad-the-individual; at the system level (Torah+prophets vs. Qurʾan+Sunna) the gap narrows sharply.

6. Christianity and Islam as systems (not just two men)

  • Christianity is constitutively about the person and work of Christ — incarnation, atonement, resurrection, Trinity, grace, church and sacraments. Its "law" is reinterpreted Torah plus the law of love; it has no divinely-mandated polity.
  • Islam is a dīn — creed plus law plus community: right belief (ʿaqīda), a revealed legal system (Sharīʿa), and a social order. Salvation is by God's mercy upon faith and deeds.
  • So they are *different kinds of thing: Christianity centers on a person to be united with; Islam on a revealed pattern of life to be followed. Most "who is better" arguments quietly assume the rival's category — a category error* (Methodology §4).

Arbiter verdict — Muhammad vs. Jesus, and the systems

Present. Polemics: "Jesus taught love, Muhammad taught the sword" vs. "the Bible is more violent than the Qurʾan." Each is a one-sided cut.

Weigh.

  • Large shared ethic: monotheism, charity, mercy, justice, sexual morality, final judgment — substantively overlapping.
  • Real structural divergence: type of founder — non-resistant suffering teacher vs. prophet-statesman-lawgiver. Textually clear, internally coherent on each side.
  • Symmetry decisive on "violence": Muhammad vs. Moses/Joshua/David + Torah ḥērem is the like-for-like test; the bare "Muhammad was violent" polemic fails because the Bible's sanctioned warfare is at least as severe. Jesus-the-individual's non-resistance is a genuine and distinctive datum — but it is Jesus vs. Muhammad, not Christianity vs. Islam as institutions.
  • Source symmetry: Gospels (early, shaped) and Ḥadīth/Sīra (later, authentication-debated) both need critical handling.

Judge.

  • On the shared ethical core: a draw — broadly common.
  • On "whose teaching is more peaceful?": at the individual level, a nameable point — Jesus' recorded personal ethic is distinctively non-resistant; at the system/scripture level (Torah+prophets vs. Qurʾan+Sunna) the contrast collapses toward parity by the symmetry rule. The popular knockout therefore only works if the comparison is rigged (Jesus vs. Muhammad, never Moses vs. Muhammad).
  • On *"which kind of founder/system is better?" — suffering non-resistant redeemer vs. prophet-legislator-statesman — this is a value premise (what a true revelation should* be), and the arbiter declines it (Methodology §5).
  • The salvation/identity divergence underneath is the same single seam (cap. 11/16) — not a new one.
